title: The Long March of the First Front Army
traveller: The First Front Red Army of the Chinese Communist Party
intro: After defeat in Chiang Kai-shek's Fifth Encirclement Campaign, the Chinese Communist Party abandoned its Jiangxi Soviet in October 1934. The First Front Red Army of some 86,000 troops headed west over rugged terrain, retreating from the advancing Kuomintang forces towards a new headquarters in Yan'an, Shaanxi.
ending: The First Front Army reached Yan'an on 19 October 1935 with about 8,000 survivors. Mao Zedong's leadership during the retreat brought him great prestige, and the march marked the beginning of his ascent to primacy in the Party.

stops.text: After the Red Army's defeat in the Fifth Encirclement Campaign, the Party decided on 10 October 1934 to abandon the Jiangxi Soviet and its headquarters at Ruijin. The First Front Red Army of some 86,000 troops headed west.
stops.quote: After the defeat of the Red Army in Chiang Kai-shek's Fifth Encirclement Campaign, on 10 October 1934 the CCP decided to abandon its Jiangxi Soviet and headquarters in Ruijin, Jiangxi. The First Front Red Army of some 86,000 troops headed west

stops.text: A force under Bo Gu and Otto Braun attacked the Kuomintang positions near Yudu. More than 86,000 troops, 11,000 administrative personnel and thousands of porters completed the breakout; the wounded and ill stayed behind to fight a delaying action.
stops.quote: On October 16, 1934, a force of about 130,000 soldiers and civilians under Bo Gu and Otto Braun attacked the line of Kuomintang positions near Yudu.

stops.text: Mao and more than 40,000 troops crossed the Gan River in a fleet of small boats. A rear guard of 16,000 troops had been left behind to divert the Nationalists.
stops.quote: From October 18 to 21, Mao along with more than 40,000 troops crossed the Gan River in an armada of small boats.

stops.text: At the Xiang River the army was intercepted by regular Nationalist troops and suffered heavy casualties. Of the 86,000 who left Jiangxi, only 36,000 escaped, and it is not possible to know how many losses were deaths and how many desertions.
stops.quote: Of the 86,000 Communists who attempted to break out of Jiangxi with the First Red Army, only 36,000 successfully escaped. Due to the low morale within the Red Army at the time, it is not possible to know what proportion of these losses were due to military casualties, and which proportion were due to desertion.

stops.text: Leaders met near the Hunan and Guizhou border to decide the army's direction. Zhou Enlai endorsed Mao's proposal to turn towards Guizhou, urging the others to overrule the objections of Bo Gu and Braun.
stops.quote: A meeting at Tongdao, close to the border of Hunan and Guizhou, was convened to discuss the direction of the Red Army on December 12, 1934.

stops.text: In the mountains of south-east Guizhou a second dispute arose over direction. Braun wanted eastern Guizhou, Mao wanted the west, and Zhou sided with Mao, so the army marched towards Zunyi.
stops.quote: Another dispute of the direction of the Red Army occurred soon after, once the Red Army reached Liping, in the mountains of southeast Guizhou.

stops.text: The army reached the Wu River. Bo and Braun again urged a return to western Hunan, but the suggestion was rejected, and Zhou's rule that all military plans go to the Politburo took effect at once, depriving Braun of the right to direct military affairs.
stops.quote: On January 1, 1935, the Red Army reached the Wu River.

stops.text: The army captured Zunyi, weakly defended and far from Nationalist forces, with little more than 10,000 men left. The conference there, 15 to 17 January, denounced Bo and Braun, and Mao won over the meeting.
stops.quote: On January 15 the Red Army captured Zunyi, the second largest city in Guizhou. As Mao had predicted, the city was weakly defended, and was too far from Nationalist forces to be under immediate threat of attack. By the time the Red Army occupied Zunyi, it was highly depleted, and counted little more than 10,000 men.

legs.title: Rivers, mountains and marshes to Shaanxi

stops.text: After manoeuvring through Guizhou, Sichuan and Yunnan, the army crossed the Yangtze here, finally escaping determined pursuit. It still faced mountain passes up to 4,000 metres, food shortages and hostile local ethnic groups.
stops.quote: The First Red Army crossed the Yangtze (the section of Jinsha River) on May 9, 1935, finally escaping determined pursuit

stops.text: The First Army is recorded as capturing Luding Bridge on 29 May. Official history extols this as a heroic triumph, but many historians now think the battle's difficulty was exaggerated or the incident fabricated for propaganda.
stops.quote: 29 May: The First Army captures Luding Bridge.

stops.text: The First Front Army met Zhang Guotao's Fourth Front Army. Zhang insisted on going south-west and Mao north towards Shaanxi; they could not agree, and the two armies split.
stops.quote: June–July: The First and Fourth Armies meet at Maogong. Mao and Zhang disagree on strategy, and the forces ultimately separate.

stops.text: The First Army crossed the Zoigê Marsh. It traversed several swamps and was attacked by Hui Ma clique forces under Generals Ma Bufang and Ma Buqing.
stops.quote: August: The First Army crosses the Zoigê Marsh.

stops.text: The First Army crossed the Lazikou Pass on 16 September 1935. In October it reached Shaanxi province and joined local Communist forces there, led by Liu Zhidan, Gao Gang and Xu Haidong.
stops.quote: 16 September: The First Army crosses the Lazikou Pass.

stops.text: The First Front Army arrived at Yan'an in northern Shaanxi. Only some 8,000 troops made it, and fewer than 7,000 of them had been among the original 100,000 who began the march.
stops.quote: Nevertheless, only some 8,000 troops under Mao's command, the First Front Army, ultimately made it to the final destination of Yan'an in 1935. Of these, less than 7,000 were among the original 100,000 soldiers who had started the march.

notes: The article contradicts itself on numbers and dates: the First Front Army is 86,000 or 130,000 (soldiers and civilians); departure is 10 October (timeline), 16 October (Yudu) or 'early October'; the Xiang River survivors are 36,000 yet Zunyi counts 'little more than 10,000'; the First Army arrives at Yan'an on 19 October 1935 in the lead but at Wuqizhen, 145 km away, in the timeline (I used Yan'an and left Wuqizhen out). Total length is disputed in the article's Length section and is not used. Liping has no date in the article (December 1934 is inferred from 'soon after' 12 December). Luding Bridge: the date 29 May comes from the timeline. The Zoigê attack by the Ma clique is placed there from the article's general description, not given for a particular place. Left out: Xinfeng River and Chen Jitang's safe passage (no date), the four crossings of the Chishui, the feints at Guiyang and Kunming (the army did not reach those cities), Yunnan, and the Second and Fourth armies' routes. Wp titles 'Maogong', 'Zoigê Wetland', 'Lazikou Pass' and 'Tongdao Dong Autonomous County' may need correcting by the editor. The article's Jiangxi purge figure (about 70,000 killed) is not used because it belongs to before the march.
